title: US court rules Google will not have to sell ad exchange after losing antitrust case
gist: A federal judge declined to force Google to divest its ad exchange (AdX) despite the DOJ winning its ad-tech antitrust case, marking the third of three major Google antitrust losses to end in only minimal remedies, leaving Google's market power effectively intact and free to pursue AI dominance.

themes.theme: Ad-tech antitrust ruling and remedy scope

insights.claim: Judge Leonie Brinkema ruled Google will not have to sell its online advertising exchange (previously branded AdX), rejecting the DOJ's proposed structural remedy in the ad-tech antitrust case that Google lost in 2025.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Removes the tail-risk of a forced divestiture of a core Google ad-tech asset; positive for Alphabet's ad business valuation and reduces contagion risk to its broader ad stack.
insights.locator: A US federal judge has sided with Google

insights.claim: The court found Google illegally locked publishers into using its ad exchange but did not find Google broke the law regarding tools used by advertisers, producing a mixed liability ruling.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Partial liability without structural remedy suggests future antitrust fines/behavioral changes are likely but will not materially disrupt Google's ad exchange revenue stream.
insights.quote: the court agreed that Google illegally locked publishers into using its exchange, it did not agree that Google had broken the law when it came to the tools used by advertisers
insights.locator: In this case, the DOJ and a coalition of states

insights.claim: The judge sealed the remedies order for 14 days to let parties request redactions, meaning the exact scope of fines and business-practice changes imposed on Google will not be public until roughly mid-September 2026.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Investors should watch for the unsealed order in ~2 weeks for concrete fine amounts and behavioral remedy details that could still affect Google's ad business economics.
insights.quote: Judge Leonie Brinkema has sealed the order for 14 days
insights.locator: That doesn't necessarily mean Google gets off scot-free

insights.claim: The author argues a forced ad-exchange divestiture would have sent ripple effects through Google's broader ad business and would have been a powerful signal to Big Tech, which has otherwise successfully turned back a recent wave of antitrust cases.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Signals a broader pattern of US courts favoring behavioral over structural antitrust remedies against dominant tech platforms, reducing breakup risk across the sector (Meta, Amazon, Apple included).
insights.locator: Despite the mixed ruling, the DOJ argued

themes.theme: Pattern across Google's three antitrust losses

insights.claim: This ad-tech case is the third of three major Google antitrust cases to reach a conclusion, and in all three Google is emerging with its market power largely unchanged despite losing each case.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: A pattern of losses-without-consequence across three separate antitrust actions strengthens the case that Google's core business model and moat face limited near-term regulatory risk in the US.
insights.quote: Google is emerging from this era of legal uncertainty largely unscathed
insights.locator: This is the third of three Google antitrust cases

insights.claim: In the DOJ's search antitrust case, Google avoided being forced to sell Chrome; the remedy instead required Google to make search data available to competitors and stop requiring partners to distribute Google apps on mobile devices.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google retains full ownership of Chrome, a critical distribution and data asset for its search and ad business and an increasingly important AI browser surface.
insights.locator: The DOJ's other case against Google

insights.claim: In the Epic Games case over Android/Play Store practices, remedies are limited to the US only, Google retains control over app vetting, but Google has already lowered Play Store fees and allowed alternative payment platforms and third-party app store distribution.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Of the three cases, the Epic ruling produces the most concrete near-term business changes (lower Play fees, alternative payments) — a modest but real drag on Google Play services revenue, contained to the US market.
insights.locator: The other antitrust case was brought by Epic Games

insights.claim: The author concludes that with its market power intact after all three cases, Google is now free to pursue building new monopolies in AI, and the current DOJ does not appear interested in standing in the way of Big Tech.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: A weakly-enforced antitrust environment implies Google (and Big Tech generally) can consolidate AI market position with reduced fear of near-term US regulatory breakup risk — relevant to competitive positioning versus OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs.
insights.quote: That frees the company up to try to build new monopolies in AI, and the current DOJ doesn't seem very interested in standing in the way of Big Tech.
insights.locator: After all these years of hearings, appeals, and decisions
